questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer on his right hand with a black eschar and surrounding non-pitting oedema. He reports handling animal hides. Gram stain of the exudate shows large Gram-positive rods in chains. Which of the following is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: This is cutaneous anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis. Penicillin G is the drug of choice for cutaneous anthrax. Doxycycline and ciprofloxacin are alternatives used in bioterrorism scenarios where penicillin resistance is suspected.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with rapidly spreading black necrotic skin lesion over his scrotum and perineum, with fever and crepitus on palpation. He is a diabetic. Blood cultures are pending. What is the most appropriate initial management?
opts: Emergency surgical debridement with broad-spectrum antibiotics
questions.exp: This is Fournier's gangrene (necrotising fasciitis of genitalia). It is a surgical emergency requiring immediate radical debridement along with broad-spectrum antibiotics targeting polymicrobial flora. Delay increases mortality significantly.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with honey-coloured crusted plaques around the nose and mouth. Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. Which organism is most likely responsible, and what is the first-line topical treatment?
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus (and sometimes Streptococcus pyogenes). Topical mupirocin is the first-line treatment for localised impetigo and is highly effective against Staphylococcal strains.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with itching and scaling of the scalp, eyebrows, and nasolabial folds. KOH examination shows Malassezia spores and hyphae. Which antifungal shampoo is most effective for long-term maintenance?
questions.exp: Seborrhoeic dermatitis is caused by Malassezia (Pityrosporum) species. Ketoconazole 2% shampoo is the most effective antifungal for long-term control of seborrhoeic dermatitis on the scalp and face.

questions.q: A 40-year-old immunocompromised patient presents with fever, skin papules with central umbilication, and pulmonary infiltrates. India ink preparation of CSF is positive. What is the systemic treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Disseminated cryptococcosis with CNS involvement in immunocompromised patients is treated with Amphotericin B (with or without flucytosine) as induction therapy. Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis carries high mortality and requires fungicidal therapy.

questions.q: A 14-year-old boy presents with scaling patches on the scalp, associated with broken hair stubs ('black dot' pattern) and cervical lymphadenopathy. KOH shows endothrix type infection. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Black dot tinea capitis is characterised by endothrix infection where hair shafts are packed with arthrospores causing them to break at the scalp level. Trichophyton tonsurans and Trichophyton violaceum are the main causes of endothrix (black dot) tinea capitis.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on her right thigh, preceded by 3 days of burning pain. She reports a similar episode 6 months ago. Which antiviral drug is used for suppressive therapy to prevent recurrences?
questions.exp: Valacyclovir 500 mg once daily is the preferred suppressive therapy for genital herpes with frequent recurrences (≥6/year). It achieves higher plasma acyclovir levels than oral acyclovir and improves compliance. Acyclovir 400 mg BD is also effective but less convenient.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with painful dermatomal vesicular eruption over his right chest wall, preceded by 2 days of hyperaesthesia. He has no known immunodeficiency. On examination, the vesicles do not cross the midline. Which complication is most feared in elderly patients with this condition?
questions.exp: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is the most common and feared complication of herpes zoster, especially in elderly patients. It is defined as pain persisting beyond 90 days after rash onset. Early antiviral therapy reduces but does not eliminate the risk of PHN.

questions.q: A neonate develops widespread blistering and skin peeling within 48 hours of birth. The mother has a history of genital HSV. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. What is the immediate treatment?
questions.exp: Neonatal herpes is a medical emergency with high mortality. IV acyclovir 20 mg/kg every 8 hours for 14-21 days is the treatment of choice. Oral formulations are not appropriate for neonatal disseminated or CNS disease.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with a painless indurated ulcer on the glans penis that appeared 3 weeks ago. VDRL is reactive and TPHA is positive. Dark field microscopy shows spirochaetes. What is the stage and treatment?
opts: Secondary syphilis; benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU single dose
Primary syphilis; benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU single dose
Primary syphilis; aqueous crystalline penicillin G for 10 days
Primary syphilis; doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days
questions.exp: The painless, indurated genital ulcer (chancre) with positive serology and dark field microscopy confirms primary syphilis. Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose is the treatment of choice for primary syphilis.

questions.q: A 23-year-old woman presents with painful inguinal lymphadenopathy with a groove sign and genital ulcers. Frei test is positive. What is the causative organism and the drug of choice?
questions.exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3. The groove sign (inguinal groove between inguinal and femoral nodes) is pathognomonic. Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days is the treatment of choice.

questions.q: A 32-year-old male presents with painless, beefy-red, moist ulcers on the genitals with rolled edges. No lymphadenopathy is noted. Donovan bodies are seen on crush preparation. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. Azithromycin 1 g weekly (or 500 mg daily) is now the preferred treatment due to convenience and efficacy. Treatment should continue until all lesions have healed completely.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man from rural India presents with hypopigmented anaesthetic patches on his forearms with thickened peripheral nerves. Slit skin smear shows no AFB. What is the classification of this leprosy and the treatment regimen?
opts: Multibacillary leprosy; rifampicin + dapsone + clofazimine for 12 months
Paucibacillary leprosy; rifampicin + dapsone for 6 months
Borderline tuberculoid; rifampicin + dapsone for 6 months
Indeterminate leprosy; dapsone monotherapy for 2 years
questions.exp: Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy with negative slit skin smear is treated with WHO MDT regimen: rifampicin 600 mg monthly (supervised) + dapsone 100 mg daily for 6 months. This covers TT and BT forms.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on treatment develops sudden erythema and oedema of existing skin lesions, with fever and painful nerve tenderness, but no new lesions. There is no iritis or orchitis. What is this reaction and its management?
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction involves upgrading CMI, causing acute inflammation of existing lesions with nerve involvement. Management is prednisolone starting at 40 mg/day and tapering over 12-24 weeks. Thalidomide is used for ENL (Type 2 reaction).

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with butterfly rash over the malar area, photosensitivity, alopecia, oral ulcers, and arthralgia. ANA is positive with anti-dsDNA antibodies. Which complement pathway component is most characteristically depleted?
questions.exp: In SLE, complement consumption primarily depletes early complement components. C1q deficiency is strongly associated with SLE pathogenesis, and low C1q, C3, and C4 are markers of active disease. C1q and C4 tend to be lowest in active lupus.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with thickening and hardening of facial and hand skin, Raynaud's phenomenon, dysphagia, and telangiectasias. Anti-Scl-70 antibody is positive. What does anti-Scl-70 target?
questions.exp: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) targets DNA topoisomerase I and is associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis with higher risk of interstitial lung disease. Anti-centromere antibody is associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome).

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with proximal muscle weakness, V-sign erythema on the neck, heliotrope rash around the eyes, and Gottron's papules over the knuckles. CK is markedly elevated. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis is an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy. Systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day) are the first-line treatment. Steroid-sparing agents like azathioprine or methotrexate are added for maintenance or steroid-resistant disease.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with blisters arising on normal skin in the axillae and groin. The blisters are tense and do not rupture easily. Nikolsky sign is negative. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 deposition at the DEJ. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid is characterised by tense blisters on normal or erythematous skin, negative Nikolsky sign, and linear IgG/C3 at the DEJ on DIF. Target antigens are BP180 and BP230 (hemidesmosomes). It is the most common autoimmune blistering disorder.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with flaccid blisters on the oral mucosa and skin. Blisters rupture easily leaving raw erosions. Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF shows intercellular IgG in a fishnet pattern. What is the target antigen?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris involves autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 (and desmoglein 1 in skin involvement). Desmoglein 3 is predominantly in mucous membranes. The suprabasal acantholysis results in flaccid blisters with positive Nikolsky sign.

questions.q: A 12-year-old child presents with intensely pruritic vesicles symmetrically distributed over the elbows, knees, and buttocks. DIF shows granular IgA at the dermal papilla tips. What is the associated systemic condition?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (Duhring's disease) is strongly associated with coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy). Granular IgA deposits at dermal papilla tips is pathognomonic. Gluten-free diet is the definitive treatment, with dapsone for symptomatic relief.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with a pearly, shiny nodule with rolled edges and central ulceration on his nose. He has a history of chronic sun exposure. Biopsy shows tumour cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artefact. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Wide local excision with 5 mm margins
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) on the nose (H-zone) is considered high-risk. Mohs micrographic surgery provides the highest cure rate and maximum tissue conservation. It allows real-time histological margin control, which is critical for facial/H-zone BCCs.

questions.q: A 45-year-old fair-skinned man presents with a rapidly enlarging, dome-shaped nodule on his forearm with a central keratin-filled crater. The lesion appeared over 6 weeks. Biopsy shows well-differentiated squamous proliferation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma is a rapidly growing tumour that typically regresses spontaneously over months. It appears as a dome-shaped nodule with a central keratin plug. Though often self-limiting, it is considered by many to be a low-grade SCC variant and surgical excision is recommended.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with an asymmetric, multicoloured lesion (brown, black, red, white areas) on her back with irregular borders, diameter of 8 mm. Dermoscopy shows atypical pigment network and irregular streaks. What is the next step?
opts: Full-thickness excision biopsy with 2 mm margin
Topical imiquimod and review in 3 months
questions.exp: A suspicious pigmented lesion (ABCDE criteria positive, suspicious dermoscopy) requires full-thickness excision biopsy with a 2 mm margin to allow accurate Breslow thickness measurement. Shave biopsy is inadequate as it may not capture the base; punch biopsy may miss the deepest part.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with itching patches of erythema, scaling, and thickened plaques on the trunk for 5 years. Biopsy shows Pautrier microabscesses in the epidermis with atypical lymphocytes. What is the first-line treatment for early stage disease?
questions.exp: Mycosis fungoides (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma) in early stage (IA-IIA) is treated with skin-directed therapies. Narrow-band UVB is first-line for patch-stage disease. PUVA, topical nitrogen mustard, and topical steroids are alternatives. Chemotherapy is reserved for advanced disease.

questions.q: A dermatologist performs photodynamic therapy (PDT) for actinic keratoses on the face. Which photosensitiser is most commonly used topically in PDT?
questions.exp: 5-Aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) and its methyl ester (MAL) are the most commonly used topical photosensitisers in PDT. They are pro-drugs converted to protoporphyrin IX (PpIX) in the skin. PDT is highly effective for actinic keratoses, Bowen's disease, and superficial BCCs.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman wants treatment for melasma. Dermatologist considers chemical peeling. Which peeling agent at appropriate concentrations is FDA-approved and most commonly used for melasma?
questions.exp: Glycolic acid (alpha-hydroxy acid) peels at concentrations of 30-70% are the most commonly used and well-studied superficial chemical peels for melasma. They are generally safe, have a short recovery time, and can be combined with bleaching agents for better outcomes.

questions.q: A patient with recalcitrant plaque psoriasis is started on methotrexate. Before starting therapy, which baseline investigation is most important to monitor hepatotoxicity?
questions.exp: Baseline LFTs, renal function, FBC, and FibroScan (hepatic elastography) are recommended before starting methotrexate. Procollagen III peptide (P-III-NP) can monitor hepatic fibrosis non-invasively in patients on long-term methotrexate, but baseline LFTs and FibroScan are standard before initiation.

questions.q: A 40-year-old psoriasis patient develops renal impairment after 2 years on cyclosporine. What is the maximum recommended duration of continuous cyclosporine therapy for psoriasis?
questions.exp: Continuous cyclosporine therapy for psoriasis should not exceed 12 months due to risk of cumulative nephrotoxicity. Cyclosporine causes dose-dependent and time-dependent nephrotoxicity. Intermittent or rotational therapy is recommended to minimise renal risk.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman with acne vulgaris is prescribed isotretinoin. She wants to become pregnant in future. What is the required washout period after stopping isotretinoin before conception?
questions.exp: Isotretinoin has a short half-life (10-20 hours) and is eliminated within 1 month of stopping. Standard guidelines recommend waiting at least 1 month after the last dose before conception. The iPLEDGE program in the US requires 1 month contraception after stopping.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of urticarial plaques, angioedema, and abdominal pain without an identifiable allergen trigger. C4 levels are persistently low. C1-inhibitor level and function are reduced. What is the diagnosis and the prophylactic treatment?
opts: Hereditary angioedema; tranexamic acid or danazol
questions.exp: Hereditary angioedema (HAE) due to C1-inhibitor deficiency presents with recurrent angioedema, urticarial plaques, and abdominal pain. Persistently low C4 (even between attacks) is characteristic. Long-term prophylaxis includes danazol (attenuated androgen) or tranexamic acid. C1-INH concentrate is used for acute attacks.
